2. Precisely, the facts of the case are that in August
2023, proposed accused Muhammad Akhtar son of
through his associate Muhammad Ismail, approached
body: the petitioner regarding the River Icon Project situated at River Garden, Expressway, Islamabad. Muhammad Akhtar represented that he held shares in the project and offered the petitioner a 50% share therein. He assured the petitioner that his investment would remain fully secured and, for that purpose, agreed to execute a Power of Attorney in favour of the petitioner. He further requested the petitioner's assistance in ongoing litigation and related matters against Gulf Alliance. Consequently, on 01.08.2023, an agreement was executed between Muhammad Akhtar and the petitioner, followed by the execution of a Power of Attorney in favour of the petitioner. After persistent efforts extending over approximately six months, a Settlement Agreement was executed on 03.01.2024 24.06.2026 Raja Rizwan Abbasi, Advocate for the petitioner. between Muhammad Akhtar and Gulf Alliance through its representatives, namely Majid Saleem, Irfan Alam and Wali Ullah, whereby the disputes relating to the River Icon Project were amicably resolved. Pursuant thereto, the project came under the joint ownership of three partners/shareholders and a Joint Venture Agreement was executed regulating the future management and operation of the project. Under the settlement arrangement, Gulf Alliance furnished an account summary pertaining to the period from January 2020 to October 2022, which was incorporated into the Settlement Agreement. The settlement documents, along with all relevant records, were submitted before the competent Court in the presence of all concerned parties. That under the terms of the Joint Venture Agreement, the River Icon Project comprising 98 residential apartments was to be completed within two years. It was specifically agreed that all amounts received from purchasers and investors would be deposited into a designated joint project account and utilized exclusively for construction and development of the project. Upon completion of the project, the accounts were to be reconciled and profits distributed among the partners in accordance with the agreed terms. Allegedly, contrary to the aforesaid arrangement and in violation of the Joint Venture Agreement, the accused persons, acting with dishonest and mala fide intent, allegedly opened and operated separate bank accounts, including accounts maintained in the names of Gulf Alliance (ABL), Gulf Alliance (UBL) and Wali Ullah (ABL), and diverted payments received from purchasers and investors into those accounts instead of the designated joint project account. As a result, substantial amounts running into crores of rupees were allegedly misappropriated and embezzled.

3. The petitioner approached the Ex-Officio Justice of Peace/Sessions Judge, by filing petition under sections 22-A and 22-B, Cr.P.C for issuance of direction to the concerned SHO to lodge FIR against the proposed accused persons. The learned Ex-Officio Justice of Peace/Sessions Judge, after hearing learned counsel for the petitioner, declined the prayer of the petitioner with regard to lodging the FIR.

4. Learned counsel for the petitioner submits that despite clear contractual obligations, the accused persons acted dishonestly and in breach of the agreed terms by opening and operating separate bank accounts in the names of Gulf Alliance and other individuals, including accounts maintained with Allied Bank Limited and United Bank Limited and that instead of depositing investors' funds into the designated joint account, they allegedly diverted such funds to their personal and unauthorized accounts and thereby misappropriated substantial amounts belonging to the project. It is further submitted that the proposed accused are habitual fraudsters and are reportedly involved in several criminal cases relating to cheating, fraud and criminal breach of trust. Despite repeated requests and demands, they have failed to furnish a proper audit of the project accounts or disclose the utilization of the funds received from investors, which, according to learned counsel, clearly demonstrates their dishonest intention and supports the allegations of criminal misappropriation and breach of trust. While arguing on the strength of the aforesaid facts, learned counsel submits that the matter discloses cognizable offences warranting a thorough investigation in accordance with law and that the conduct of the accused persons has caused substantial financial loss not only to the petitioner but also to numerous investors associated with the project, however, learned Ex.Officio Justice of Peace has acted in a mechanical manner while dismissing the petition vide impugned order, which is not sustainable in the eyes of law.

6. A perusal of the impugned order dated 15.06.2026 reveals that it is a comprehensive, wellreasoned, and self-speaking order addressing all material aspects of the controversy. The petitioner was unable to dispute or rebut the admitted factum of his joint business association with the proposed accused persons. It is also an undisputed position that the disputes between the parties are already sub judice before a competent Civil Court, where the relevant record pertaining to the accounts has been produced and is presently under consideration. In such circumstances, the contention of the learned counsel for the petitioner seeking a direction for audit of accounts through the police loses much of its significance, as the determination of matters relating to rendition of accounts, settlement of financial liabilities, and examination of business transactions squarely falls within the domain and competence of the Civil Court. Therefore, in the prevailing factual and legal backdrop, the learned Ex-Officio Justice of Peace was fully justified in observing that, unless and until a definitive finding is rendered by the competent Civil Court regarding the alleged embezzlement or misappropriation of any amount by the proposed accused persons, no direction for initiation of criminal proceedings or further action could validly be issued.

7. It is settled law that directions for registration of an FIR should not be issued as a matter of course. In "Munawar Alam Khan v. Qurban Ali Mallono" (2024 SCMR 985) the Supreme Court held that applications filed under Sections 22-A and 22-B Cr.P.C. must not be lightly entertained and should not be decided in a mechanical manner by issuing directions to the police to lodge an FIR. Where the allegations are unsupported by any prima facie material and serious doubts exist regarding their veracity, the Justice of Peace is competent to decline such relief.

8. Furthermore, the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan in “Jamal Khan vs. Secretary Home Department” (2021 SCMR 468) declined to interfere in criminal findings refusing registration of a case where the underlying dispute essentially civil in nature.

9. Prima facie, it is a dispute of civil nature between the parties. Despite the fact that the petitioner had remedy of filing private complaint before the learned Court concerned but he is trying to convert the same into criminal liability, which has been criticized by the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan in a case titled “Rai Ashraf and others v. Muhammad Saleem Bhatti and others” (PLD 2010 SC 691).

10. Learned Ex.Officio Justice of Peace requisitioned the report from Superintendent of Police (Complaints) Islamabad, who also reported that the matter between the parties is of civil nature whereas civil suit is pending adjudication before Raja Waqas, learned Civil Judge Islamabad. In the attending circumstances, the learned Ex-Officio Justice of Peace had no other option except to consider the report and parawise comments furnished by the Superintendent of Police concerned. Even otherwise, the report and parawise comments furnished by the police cannot be brushed aside if requisitioned by the learned trial court. Guidance is sought from“Khizer Hayat and others v. Inspector General of Police (Punjab) Lahore and others” (PLD 2005 Lahore 470). The Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of "Habibullah v. Political Assistant, Dera Ghazi Khan and others" (2005 SCMR 951), has observed that filing of private complaint could provide an equal adequate relief to the petitioner because he could lead the entire evidence himself before the Trial Court and his grievance could be adequately redressed considering also the fact that respondent/SHO, who in the report and para-wise comments has mentioned adverse to the petitioner's case, therefore, it could not be expected from the concerned SHO that he would carry independent and impartial investigation in the case.

11. In view of above, this Court found no legal infirmity, irregularity or jurisdictional error in the order dated 15.06.2026. Therefore, this petition, having no force, is dismissed in limine. However, the petitioner has alternate remedy, if so advised.
Shamroz Ali* APPROVED FOR REPORTING (CHIEF JUSTICE)
